paper_metadata.title: LARGE-SCALE PORTFOLIO OPTIMIZATION USING PAULI CORRELATION ENCODING

summary: The paper proposes a gate‑based variational portfolio optimization method using Pauli Correlation Encoding (PCE) that encodes multiple variables per qubit, enabling experiments on S&P 500 subsets up to 250 assets using only 9 qubits on a statevector simulator. Gate counts remain under ~730 gates for PCE compared with >42,000 gates for QAOA at similar problem sizes, and the approach reportedly solves instances with ≥200 assets in about one hour of simulation while improving Sharpe ratios over the baseline portfolio.

experiments.description: Gate-based variational portfolio optimization using Pauli Correlation Encoding (PCE) with a hardware-efficient ansatz, benchmarked across S&P 500 subproblems from 10 to 250 assets and compared against QAOA for the smallest instance and a classical EDA baseline for larger instances.

algorithm.variant: Pauli Correlation Encoding (PCE) with Hardware-Efficient Ansatz
algorithm.ansatz: Hardware-Efficient Ansatz (HEA) with linear entangling structure and CZ gates
algorithm.optimizer: COBYLA (for PCE); optimizer for QAOA benchmark not specified

hyperparameters.nsplits: varied by instance size; 2, 4, 6, 9 for m < 100 and (m/10)-1 for m >= 100

algorithm.parameter_initialization: Initialize symbol map; initial parameter values not reported

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Multiple optimization variables are encoded per qubit via Pauli correlation signs; number of variables scales as O(nk) with k-th order Pauli strings
problem_formulation.objective_function: Maximize Cut(G, x) = sum_{(i,j) in E} w_ij x_i (1 - x_j) within recursive bipartitioning; portfolio selection then chooses the highest-return asset from each cluster
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Recursive bipartitioning of the market graph; no explicit penalty formulation reported

problem_instance.description: Real-world portfolio optimization on S&P 500 market graphs, recursively partitioned into sub-portfolios and evaluated on train/test splits

ticker_symbols: first m columns of the dataset for each experiment size
dataset_specification.date_range: 5 years historical data; exact dates not reported
dataset_specification.preprocessing: market graph built from pairwise Pearson correlations above threshold lambda; training set used for partitioning, testing set for evaluation

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Construct market graph with nodes as assets and edges when |rho_ij| > lambda, with edge weight w_ij = 1 - |rho_ij|; select representative asset in each cluster by highest historical return
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Benchmarking against QAOA for m=10 and EDA for larger instances; performance evaluated by portfolio value over time and Sharpe ratio on train and test sets; runtime analysis for a single iteration with nsplits=1

implementation_details.classical_solver: COBYLA optimizer for PCE variational training; classical baseline method is Estimation of Distribution Algorithms (EDA)
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Statevector simulation used for measurements; recursive graph partitioning; train/test split; representative asset selection by maximum return within each cluster
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Construct final portfolio from selected representatives and evaluate portfolio value and Sharpe ratio
implementation_details.total_execution_time: PCE solves m >= 200 in approximately one hour (statevector simulation); exact per-instance times not fully reported

speedup_claims.factor: PCE gate count remains under 750 gates up to 250 assets, versus QAOA reaching 42,646 gates at 250 assets
speedup_claims.conditions: Table 2 comparison; QAOA shown for p = 1 and p = 2, PCE for k = 2 and k = 3
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a gate-count/resource comparison, not a proven runtime or asymptotic speedup; QAOA and PCE are evaluated on different encodings and depths.

speedup_claims.factor: PCE solves m >= 200 in approximately one hour on statevector simulation
speedup_claims.conditions: Single-iteration runtime analysis with nsplits = 1; statevector simulation
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper states QAOA has the highest computational cost, but does not provide a direct numeric runtime for QAOA at the same sizes in text.

speedup_claims.factor: Scalability beyond conventional one-qubit-per-asset gate-based methods
speedup_claims.conditions: Using Pauli Correlation Encoding with multiple variables per qubit
speedup_claims.caveats: The paper claims improved scalability and potential to accommodate the full S&P 500 or larger asset sets, but no formal speedup proof is given.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: PCE encoding scales as O(nk); circuit depth does not depend on target problem size in the same way as QAOA

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Would require substantially larger logical quantum hardware than the simulated 4–9 qubits and a clear asymptotic speedup over classical heuristics; none is established.
limiting_factors: All experiments performed on statevector simulation
Classical heuristic (EDA) used successfully for large instances
Performance comparison focuses on portfolio returns rather than computational complexity advantage
Gate-based circuits demonstrated only with ≤9 qubits

notes: num_qubits and circuit_depth are inferred from Table 2 and the relation p = floor(m/n) with reported n values implied by the table; the paper explicitly reports gate counts and PCE scaling but not a single fixed qubit count for all instances.
hardware.type is paper_reported as statevector simulation.
QAOA and EDA are baselines, not separate experiments.
The paper suggests improved scalability of the PCE encoding relative to QAOA in gate counts but does not demonstrate runtime or solution-quality advantage over classical methods.
Experiments rely on noiseless simulation and comparison with a classical heuristic (EDA) that still performs competitively.
